{{Short description|Formulation of the principle of stationary action}}
[[File:Least action principle.svg|250px|thumb|As the system evolves, '''q''' traces a path through [[configuration space (physics)|configuration space]] (only some are shown). The path taken by the system (red) has a stationary action (δ''S'' = 0) under small changes in the configuration of the system (δ'''q''').<ref name=penrose>{{cite book |author=R. Penrose| title=[[The Road to Reality]]| publisher= Vintage books| year=2007 | page = 474|isbn=978-0-679-77631-4}}</ref>]]
{{classical mechanics}}

In [[physics]], '''Hamilton's principle''' is [[William Rowan Hamilton]]'s formulation of the [[principle of stationary action]]. It states that the [[dynamics (mechanics)|dynamics]] of a physical system are determined by a [[calculus of variations|variational problem]] for a [[functional (mathematics)|functional]] based on a single function, the [[Lagrangian mechanics|Lagrangian]], which may contain all physical information concerning the system and the forces acting on it. The variational problem is equivalent to and allows for the derivation of the ''[[differential equation|differential]]'' [[equations of motion]] of the physical system.  Although formulated originally for [[classical mechanics]], Hamilton's principle also applies to classical [[field (physics)|fields]] such as the [[electromagnetism|electromagnetic]] and [[gravity|gravitational]] [[field (physics)|fields]], and plays an important role in [[quantum mechanics]], [[quantum field theory]] and criticality theories.

==Mathematical formulation==

Hamilton's principle states that the true evolution {{math|'''q'''(''t'')}} of a system described by {{mvar|N}} [[generalized coordinates]] {{math|1='''q''' = (''q''<sub>1</sub>, ''q''<sub>2</sub>, ..., ''q''<sub>''N''</sub>)}} between two specified states {{math|1='''q'''<sub>1</sub> = '''q'''(''t''<sub>1</sub>)}} and {{math|1='''q'''<sub>2</sub> = '''q'''(''t''<sub>2</sub>)}} at two specified times {{math|''t''<sub>1</sub>}} and {{math|''t''<sub>2</sub>}} is a [[stationary point]] (a point where the [[Calculus of variations|variation]] is zero) of the [[action (physics)|action]] [[functional (mathematics)|functional]]
<math display="block">
\mathcal{S}[\mathbf{q}] \ \stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=}\  
\int_{t_1}^{t_2} L(\mathbf{q}(t),\dot{\mathbf{q}}(t),t)\, dt 
</math>
where <math>L(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}},t)</math> is the [[Lagrangian mechanics|Lagrangian]] [[function (mathematics)|function]] for the system.  In other words, any ''first-order'' perturbation of the true evolution results in (at most) ''second-order'' changes in <math>\mathcal{S}</math>.  The action <math>\mathcal{S}</math> is a [[functional (mathematics)|functional]], i.e., something that takes as its input a [[function (mathematics)|function]] and returns a single number, a [[scalar (physics)|scalar]].  In terms of [[functional analysis]], Hamilton's principle states that the true evolution of a physical system is a solution of the functional equation

{{Equation box 1
|indent =:
|title='''Hamilton's principle'''
|equation = <math>
\frac{\delta \mathcal{S}}{\delta \mathbf{q}(t)}=0.
</math>
|border=2
|border colour = #50C878
|background colour = #ECFCF4}}

That is, the system takes a path in configuration space for which the action is stationary, with fixed boundary conditions at the beginning and the end of the path.

===Derivation from Newton's laws of motion===
Although Hamilton's principle can be viewed as a postulate effectively replacing Newton's laws of motion,<ref name="y446">{{cite book | last1=Butterfield | first1=Jeremy | last2=Earman | first2=John | title=Philosophy of Physics | publisher=Elsevier | publication-place=Amsterdam | date=2007 | isbn=978-0-444-51560-5 | page=}}</ref> it can also be derived from Newton's laws.<ref name="y752">{{cite book | last=Goldstein | first=Herbert | title=Classical Mechanics | publisher=Pearson Education India | date=2011 | isbn=978-81-317-5891-5 | page=}}</ref>{{rp|44}} Starting with [[d'Alembert's principle]]:

<math display="block">\sum_{i} ( \mathbf {F}_{i} - m_i \mathbf{a}_i )\cdot \delta \mathbf r_i = 0.</math>

Where <math>i</math> is the index of a mass, <math>\mathbf {F}_i</math> is applied force (excluding constraint forces), <math>\textbf a_i</math> is acceleration of the mass, and <math>\delta \mathbf r_i</math> is the virtual displacement of the <math>i</math>-th mass consistent with the constraints. The above equation holds true for all times <math>t</math> so a definite integral with respect to <math>t</math> must also be 0:

<math display="block">\int_{t_1}^{t_2} \sum_{i} ( \mathbf {F}_{i} - m_i \ddot \mathbf{r}_i )\cdot \delta \mathbf r_i dt = 0.</math>

<math>\delta \mathbf r_i</math>, the sum, and the integral can all be distributed:

<math display="block">\int_{t_1}^{t_2} \sum_i \mathbf{F}_i \cdot \delta \mathbf{r}_i dt - \int_{t_1}^{t_2}\sum_i m_i \ddot{\mathbf{r}}_i \cdot \delta \mathbf{r}_i dt = 0</math>

Looking at the second term we can use the [[product rule]] to find the relation:

<math display="block">\frac{d}{dt} (m_i \dot{\mathbf{r}}_i \cdot \delta \mathbf{r}_i) = m_i \ddot{\mathbf{r}}_i \cdot \delta \mathbf{r}_i + m_i \dot{\mathbf{r}}_i \cdot \frac{d}{dt}(\delta \mathbf{r}_i)</math>

Variation <math>\delta</math> and the time derivative <math>\frac{d}{dt}</math> commute (meaning <math>\frac{d}{dt}\delta \mathbf{r} = \delta \dot{\mathbf{r}}</math>), so we can rearrange this to isolate our acceleration term:

<math display="block">m_i \ddot{\mathbf{r}}_i \cdot \delta \mathbf{r}_i = \frac{d}{dt} (m_i \dot{\mathbf{r}}_i \cdot \delta \mathbf{r}_i) - m_i \dot{\mathbf{r}}_i \cdot \delta \dot{\mathbf{r}}_i</math>

Substituting this into the integral we get:

<math display="block">\int_{t_1}^{t_2} \sum_i m_i \ddot{\mathbf{r}}_i \cdot \delta \mathbf{r}_i \, dt = \sum_i \left[ m_i \dot{\mathbf{r}}_i \cdot \delta \mathbf{r}_i \right]_{t_1}^{t_2} - \int_{t_1}^{t_2} \sum_i m_i \dot{\mathbf{r}}_i \cdot \delta \dot{\mathbf{r}}_i \, dt</math>

In Hamilton's principle, we define the variations such that they vanish at the endpoints: <math>\delta \mathbf{r}_i(t_1) = \delta \mathbf{r}_i(t_2) = 0</math>. This makes the first term on the right disappear completely. Also <math>\delta(\dot \mathbf r^2)=2\dot \mathbf r \cdot \delta \dot \mathbf r</math> so the remaining term is:

<math display="block">-\int_{t_1}^{t_2} \delta \left( \sum_i \frac{1}{2} m_i \dot{\mathbf{r}}_i^2 \right) dt = - \int_{t_1}^{t_2} \delta T \, dt</math>

Where <math>T</math> is the total kinetic energy. Looking at the applied force term, if the forces are conservative, they can be derived from a potential energy <math>V(\mathbf{r}_1, \mathbf{r}_2, \dots)</math>. The work done by these forces during a virtual displacement is:

<math display="block">\sum_i \mathbf{F}_i \cdot \delta \mathbf{r}_i = -\sum_i \nabla_i V \cdot \delta \mathbf{r}_i = -\delta V</math>

Substituting everything back into the integral gives:

<math display="block">\int_{t_1}^{t_2} (-\delta V - (-\delta T)) \, dt = 0</math>
<math display="block">\delta \int_{t_1}^{t_2} (T - V) \, dt = 0</math>

Here the Lagrangian <math>L=T-V</math>. This is Hamilton's principle for a non-relativistic system of masses in the absence of an electromagnetic field.<ref>{{cite book |last=Torby |first=Bruce |title=Advanced Dynamics for Engineers |series=HRW Series in Mechanical Engineering |year=1984 |publisher=CBS College Publishing |location=United States of America  |isbn=0-03-063366-4 |chapter=Energy Methods}}</ref>

===Euler–Lagrange equations derived from the action integral===
{{Main | Euler–Lagrange equation}}

Requiring that the true trajectory {{math|'''q'''(''t'')}} be a [[stationary point]] of the action functional <math>\mathcal{S}</math> is equivalent to a set of differential equations for {{math|'''q'''(''t'')}} (the '''Euler–Lagrange equations'''), which may be derived as follows.

Let {{math|'''q'''(''t'')}} represent the true evolution of the system between two specified states {{math|1='''q'''<sub>1</sub> = '''q'''(''t''<sub>1</sub>)}} and {{math|1='''q'''<sub>2</sub> = '''q'''(''t''<sub>2</sub>)}} at two specified times {{math|''t''<sub>1</sub>}} and {{math|''t''<sub>2</sub>}}, and let {{math|'''ε'''(''t'')}} be a small perturbation that is zero at the endpoints of the trajectory
<math display="block">\boldsymbol\varepsilon(t_1) = \boldsymbol\varepsilon(t_2) \ \stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=}\  0</math>

To first order in the perturbation {{math|'''ε'''(''t'')}}, the change in the action functional <math>\delta\mathcal{S}</math> would be
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\delta \mathcal{S} &=
\int_{t_1}^{t_2}\;
\left[ L(\mathbf{q}+\boldsymbol\varepsilon,\dot{\mathbf{q}} +\dot{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}})- L(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}}) \right]dt \\
&= \int_{t_1}^{t_2}\; \left(
\boldsymbol\varepsilon \cdot \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{q}} + 
\dot{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}} \cdot \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{\mathbf{q}}}  \right)\,dt      
\end{align}</math>
where we have expanded the [[Lagrangian mechanics|Lagrangian]] ''L'' to first order in the perturbation {{math|'''ε'''(''t'')}}.

Applying [[integration by parts]] to the last term results in
<math display="block">
\delta \mathcal{S} = 
\left[ \boldsymbol\varepsilon \cdot \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{\mathbf{q}}}\right]_{t_1}^{t_2} + 
\int_{t_1}^{t_2}\; 
\left( \boldsymbol\varepsilon \cdot \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{q}}
- \boldsymbol\varepsilon \cdot \frac{d}{dt} \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{\mathbf{q}}} \right)\,dt
</math>

The boundary conditions <math>\boldsymbol\varepsilon(t_1) = \boldsymbol\varepsilon(t_2) \ \stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=}\ 0</math> causes the first term to vanish
<math display="block">\delta \mathcal{S} = \int_{t_1}^{t_2}\; \boldsymbol\varepsilon \cdot\left(\frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{q}} - \frac{d}{dt} \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{\mathbf{q}}} \right)\,dt</math>

Hamilton's principle requires that this first-order change <math>\delta \mathcal{S}</math> is zero for all possible perturbations {{math|'''ε'''(''t'')}}, i.e., the true path is a [[stationary point]] of the action functional <math>\mathcal{S}</math> (either a minimum, maximum or saddle point).  This requirement can be satisfied if and only if

{{Equation box 1
|indent =:
|title='''[[Euler–Lagrange equations]]'''
|equation = <math> \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{q}} - \frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{\mathbf{q}}} = 0</math>
|border=2
|border colour = #0073CF
|background colour=#F5FFFA}}

These equations are called the Euler–Lagrange equations for the variational problem.

===Example: Free particle in polar coordinates===

Trivial examples help to appreciate the use of the action principle via the Euler–Lagrange equations. A free particle (mass ''m'' and velocity ''v'') in Euclidean space moves in a straight line. Using the Euler–Lagrange equations, this can be shown in [[coordinates (elementary mathematics)|polar coordinates]] as follows. In the absence of a potential, the Lagrangian is simply equal to the kinetic energy 
<math display="block"> L = \frac{1}{2} mv^2= \frac{1}{2}m \left( \dot{x}^2 + \dot{y}^2 \right)</math>
in orthonormal (''x'',''y'') coordinates, where the dot represents differentiation with respect to the curve parameter (usually the time, ''t''). Therefore, upon application of the Euler–Lagrange equations,
<math display="block"> \frac{d}{dt} \left( \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{x}} \right) - \frac{\partial L}{\partial x} = 0 \qquad \Rightarrow  \qquad m\ddot{x} = 0 </math>

And likewise for ''y''. Thus the Euler–Lagrange formulation can be used to derive Newton's laws.

In polar coordinates {{math|(''r'', ''φ'')}} the kinetic energy and hence the Lagrangian becomes
<math display="block"> L = \frac{1}{2}m \left( \dot{r}^2 + r^2\dot{\varphi}^2 \right). </math>

The radial {{mvar|r}} and {{mvar|φ}} components of the Euler–Lagrange equations become, respectively
<math display="block">\frac{d}{dt} \left( \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{r}} \right) - \frac{\partial L}{\partial r} = 0  \qquad
\Rightarrow  \qquad \ddot{r} - r\dot{\varphi}^2 = 0 </math>
<math display="block">\frac{d}{dt} \left( \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{\varphi}}  \right)-\frac{\partial L}{\partial \varphi} = 0  \qquad
\Rightarrow  \qquad \ddot{\varphi} + \frac{2}{r}\dot{r}\dot{\varphi} = 0.</math>

remembering that r is also dependent on time and the product rule is needed to compute the total time derivative <math display="inline">\frac{d}{dt} mr^2 \dot{\varphi}</math>.

The solution of these two equations is given by
<math display="block"> r = \sqrt{(a t + b)^2 + c^2} </math>
<math display="block"> \varphi = \tan^{-1} \left( \frac{a t + b}{c} \right) + d </math>
for a set of constants {{math|''a''}}, {{math|''b''}}, {{math|''c''}}, {{math|''d''}} determined by initial conditions.
Thus, indeed, ''the solution is a straight line'' given in polar coordinates: {{math|''a''}} is the velocity, {{math|''c''}} is the distance of the closest approach to the origin, and {{math|''d''}} is the angle of motion.

==Applied to deformable bodies==
Hamilton's principle is an important variational principle in [[Linear elasticity|elastodynamics]]. As opposed to a system composed of rigid bodies, deformable bodies have an infinite number of degrees of freedom and occupy continuous regions of space; consequently, the state of the system is described by using continuous functions of space and time. The extended Hamilton Principle for such bodies is given by
<math display="block"> \int_{t_1}^{t_2} \left[ \delta W_e + \delta T - \delta U \right]dt = 0 </math>
where {{mvar|T}} is the kinetic energy, {{mvar|U}} is the elastic energy, {{math|''W''<sub>e</sub>}} is the work done by external loads on the body, and {{math|''t''<sub>1</sub>}}, {{math|''t''<sub>2</sub>}} the initial and final times. If the system is conservative, the work done by external forces may be derived from a scalar potential {{mvar|V}}. In this case,
<math display="block"> \delta \int_{t_1}^{t_2} \left[ T - (U + V) \right]dt = 0.</math>
This is called Hamilton's principle and it is invariant under coordinate transformations.

==Comparison with Maupertuis' principle==

Hamilton's principle and [[Maupertuis' principle]] are occasionally confused and both have been called the [[principle of least action]].  They differ in three important ways: 
* ''their definition of the [[action (physics)|action]]...'' {{pb}}Maupertuis' principle uses an integral over the [[generalized coordinates]] known as the '''abbreviated action''' or [[reduced action]] <math display="block">\mathcal{S}_{0} \ \stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=}\  \int \mathbf{p} \cdot d\mathbf{q}</math> where '''p''' = (''p''<sub>1</sub>, ''p''<sub>2</sub>, ..., ''p<sub>N</sub>'') are the conjugate momenta defined above.  By contrast, Hamilton's principle uses <math>\mathcal{S}</math>, the integral of the [[Lagrangian mechanics|Lagrangian]] over time.
*''the solution that they determine...'' {{pb}} Hamilton's principle determines the trajectory '''q'''(''t'') as a function of time, whereas Maupertuis' principle determines only the shape of the trajectory in the generalized coordinates.  For example, Maupertuis' principle determines the shape of the ellipse on which a particle moves under the influence of an inverse-square central force such as [[gravitation|gravity]], but does not describe ''per se'' how the particle moves along that trajectory.  (However, this time parameterization may be determined from the trajectory itself in subsequent calculations using the [[conservation of energy]]).  By contrast, Hamilton's principle directly specifies the motion along the ellipse as a function of time.
*''...and the constraints on the variation.'' {{pb}}Maupertuis' principle requires that the two endpoint states ''q''<sub>1</sub> and ''q''<sub>2</sub> be given and that energy be conserved along every trajectory (same energy for each trajectory). This forces the endpoint times to be varied as well. By contrast, Hamilton's principle does not require the conservation of energy, but does require that the endpoint times ''t''<sub>1</sub> and ''t''<sub>2</sub> be specified as well as the endpoint states ''q''<sub>1</sub> and ''q''<sub>2</sub>.

==Action principle for fields==

===Classical field theory===

{{main|Classical field theory}}

The '''action principle''' can be extended to obtain the [[equations of motion]] for [[field (physics)|fields]], such as the [[electromagnetic field]] or [[Einstein–Hilbert action|gravity]].

The [[Einstein equation]] utilizes the ''[[Einstein–Hilbert action]]'' as constrained by a [[variational principle]].

The path of a body in a gravitational field (i.e. free fall in space time, a so-called [[geodesic]]) can be found using the action principle.

===Quantum mechanics and quantum field theory===

{{main|Quantum field theory}}

In [[quantum mechanics]], the system does not follow a single path whose action is stationary, but the behavior of the system depends on all imaginable paths and the value of their action. The action corresponding to the various paths is used to calculate the [[Path integral formulation|path integral]], that gives the [[probability amplitude]]s of the various outcomes.{{cn|date=February 2026}}

Although equivalent in classical mechanics with [[Newton's laws]], the [[Action (physics)|action principle]] is better suited for generalizations and plays an important role in modern physics.  Indeed, this principle is one of the great generalizations in physical science. In particular, it is fully appreciated and best understood within [[quantum mechanics]]. [[Richard Feynman]]'s [[path integral formulation]] of quantum mechanics is based on a stationary-action principle, using path integrals. [[Maxwell's equations]] can be derived as conditions of stationary action.{{cn|date=February 2026}}
